questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct in the context of Special Drawing Rights (SDR)?

options.text: The SDR basket of currencies includes the US Dollar, Euro, Japanese Yen, Pound Sterling.
The SDR currency value is calculated on an annual basis.
The SDR was initially defined as equivalent to 0.888671 grams of fine gold.
The SDR is the currency of the IMF.

questions.solution:
**The correct answer is The SDR was initially defined as equivalent to 0.888671 grams of fine gold.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Special Drawing Right (SDR) was initially defined in 1969 by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) as equivalent to 0.888671 grams of fine gold, which, at that time, was also equivalent to one U.S. dollar.
 
• However, after the collapse of the Bretton Woods system in 1973, the SDR was redefined as a basket of currencies, today consisting of the U.S. dollar, Euro, Chinese yuan, Japanese yen, and British pound sterling. The composition of the SDR basket is reviewed every five years by the Executive Board of the IMF.
 
• It's important to remember that the SDR is not a currency or a claim on the IMF. Rather, it's a potential claim on the freely usable currencies of IMF members. SDRs can be exchanged for these currencies and are often used as an international reserve asset to supplement the official reserves of member countries.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**** Here are a few additional points about Special Drawing Rights (SDRs):**

 
• **International Reserve Asset: **The SDR was created by the IMF to supplement the official reserves of its member countries. The international reserve assets of countries were majorly composed of gold and US dollars. The SDR was introduced to add to these assets and mitigate potential risks associated with them.
 
• **Unit of Account:** The SDR is used by the IMF as a unit of account and some other international organizations as well.
 
• Allocation and Holdings: The SDRs are allocated to the countries based on their quota at the IMF. The members often hold more or fewer SDRs than their allocations depending on their economic circumstances.
 
• **Role in Financial Crisis: **During global financial crises, the role of SDRs becomes particularly important. For instance, in response to the global financial crisis in 2009, the IMF allocated a large amount of SDRs to provide liquidity to the global economic system.
 
• **Not a Currency: **Although the SDR represents a potential claim on the freely usable currencies of IMF members, it isn't a currency itself. It can't be used for transactions between governments and private parties, like traditional currency.
 
• **Recent Developments:** Recently, there have been discussions about a new allocation of SDRs due to the economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.

SDRs are an integral part of the global monetary system and play a crucial role in providing liquidity to countries, especially in times of economic crises. They contribute to global financial stability by supplementing the official reserves of countries, thereby strengthening their ability to defend their currencies against financial shocks.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements is/are true?

A - In perfect competition, average revenue is equal to market price.

B - In perfect competition, marginal revenue is equal to market price.

options.text: Both A and B are true
Neither A nor B is true

questions.solution:
**The correct answer is Both A and B are true**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** **Both statements A and B are correct in the context of perfect competition.**

 
• **A - In perfect competition, average revenue is equal to market price.**
 
• **B - In perfect competition, marginal revenue is equal to market price.**

__
 
• In a perfect competition scenario, firms are price takers, meaning they cannot influence the market price and must accept the prevailing market price for their product. Hence, they sell their goods and services at the same price to all customers.
 
• Average Revenue (AR) is total revenue divided by the number of units sold. Since the selling price is the same for all units, average revenue will equal this constant price.
 
• Marginal Revenue (MR) is the additional revenue generated by selling an extra unit of a good or service. Since the market price is constant in perfect competition, each

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** __Here are a few more key points to understanding the characteristics of perfect competition:__

 
• **Numerous Buyers and Sellers: **In a perfectly competitive market, there are many buyers and sellers. Hence, individual consumers or producers do not have the power to influence the price.
 
• **Homogeneous Product: **The products are perfect substitutes for each other. They are identical in terms of quality, size, design, features, etc.
 
• **Free Entry and Exit: **Firms can freely enter and exit the market. There are no barriers to entry or exit like licenses, patents, large capital, etc.
 
• **Perfect Knowledge: **Buyers and sellers have perfect knowledge about the prices and products of all the firms in the market. This ensures that the price does not deviate from its equilibrium.
 
• **Zero Advertising Costs: **Since the goods are homogeneous, there is no need for the firms to advertise their products.
 
• **No Government Regulation: **There are no government regulations or interventions, and no firm receives special treatment.

Because of these conditions, buyers and sellers can't affect prices individually and must accept the prevailing price. In perfect competition, firms are price-takers, not price-makers. Hence, the market determines the price according to aggregate supply and demand. As a result, a firm's average revenue, marginal revenue, and price are all equal.

questions.question: Q = L + K (where Q is output, L is labor and K is capital), depicts a production function with:

options.text: both Increasing and Constant Returns to Scale

questions.solution:
**The correct answer is Constant Returns to Scale**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The production function Q = L + K indicates constant returns to scale.
 
• In economics, returns to scale refer to the changes in output as all inputs (in this case, labor and capital) are increased proportionately. In constant returns to scale, if we double all inputs, output also doubles.
 
• This is unlike increasing returns to scale (where output more than doubles when inputs are doubled) or decreasing returns to scale (where output less than doubles when inputs are doubled).
 
• In the given production function, if you double both L and K, the output Q will double, thus suggesting constant returns to scale. For example, if L = 10 and K = 10, Q = 20. If we double L and K to 20 each, Q = 40, demonstrating constant returns to scale.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** __Here are a few more things worth noting about returns to scale:__

 
• Returns to Scale and Production Efficiency: Studying returns to scale helps businesses understand the cost-effectiveness of increasing production. If a company's production function exhibits increasing returns to scale, it may make sense to significantly boost capacity. On the other hand, if a business faces decreasing returns to scale, it might be more efficient to stay at or reduce its current production level.
 
• Long-Term Phenomenon: Returns to scale primarily relate to the long run when all factors of production are variable. This contrasts with the concept of "returns to a factor," which is a short-term phenomenon when at least one factor is fixed.
 
• Assumptions: The concept of returns to scale assumes other factors remain constant, such as technology or the managerial ability of a firm.
 
• Implications for Industry Structure: Returns to scale can influence the structure of an industry. Industries with significant increasing returns to scale can become dominated by a few large players, as the cost advantages of large-scale operations can form a barrier to entry for smaller firms. In contrast, industries with constant or decreasing returns to scale are more likely to be competitive, with many firms in operation.
 
• Relationship with Economies of Scale: While related, returns to scale and economies of scale are not the same concept. Returns to scale refer to changes in production output due to proportional increases in all inputs. Economies of scale, meanwhile, refer to the effect of increasing the scale of production on the average cost of production. With economies of scale, output increases at a faster rate than cost, thus lowering the average cost per unit.

• The decision on 'how to produce' reflects the production strategy of an economy and could potentially impact future development prospects.
 
• Along with 'what to produce' and 'for whom to produce', 'how to produce' represents one of the three central problems all economies need to solve due to the basic economic problem: the scarcity of resources.
 
• Technological advancement plays a huge role in shaping the 'how to produce' question. Economies with access to advanced technologies may opt for more capital-intensive methods as they can lead to greater efficiency, productivity, and eventual cost savings.

questions.question: Since independence, India has been a _____________.
questions.solution:
**The correct answer is a mixed economy**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Since gaining its independence in 1947, India has been a mixed economy.
 
• A mixed economy combines characteristics of both market and planned economies — it includes both capitalist and socialist structures. In a mixed economy, the government participates in economic planning and decision-making but also allows private enterprise to function.
 
• In the case of India, sectors are divided into public and private sectors. Both these sectors co-exist and function together. The public sector tends to be reserved for industries deemed essential or sensitive (such as defense, infrastructure, and energy), and the private sector operates in other fields under regulations defined by the government.
 
• The principle of a mixed economy in India was enshrined in the country's constitution after independence and continues to shape its economic policies till now.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__** Here are some additional points about India as a mixed economy:

 
• **Post-independence Economy: **Initially following independence, India adopted an economic policy of self-sufficiency, with heavy regulations and protectionist policies, plus a large emphasis on public sector undertakings (PSUs).
 
• **Economic Liberalization: **In 1991, facing a severe economic crisis, India embarked on a process of liberalization and economic reforms. This resulted in a lessening of government regulations and controls over the economy, opened sectors for private enterprises, and made a marked shift toward a more market-oriented economy. However, India still retained its mixed economy structure, with the co-existence of both public and private sectors.
 
• **Public Sector Dominance: **Despite liberalization, the Indian government still holds a dominant position in several key sectors such as defense, electricity, and railways, amongst others.
 
• **Welfare State: **A major characteristic of a mixed economy is that while wealth generation is important, it is also necessary to work towards societal equity. India, as a mixed economy, strives to achieve this balance. The state often intervenes to prevent business malpractices, reduce inequality, and provide public welfare in the form of various schemes and programs.
 
• **Role of Private Sector: **Over time, the private sector in India has gained substantial importance with its contribution to the Indian economy. It has not only led to improving the GDP and providing employment opportunities but also to technological advancements and innovation.
 
• **Foreign Investment: **India's mixed economy allows Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in various sectors. This strategy has helped in the growth and development of the economy, brought in advanced technologies, and created jobs.

Remember, the structure of a mixed economy offers flexibility and can vary greatly from country to country, reflecting the balance that its society and government have chosen between free markets and state control.

questions.question: ____________ happens when a government sells only a part of its stake in a public sector company and retains the majority of it.
questions.solution:
**The correct answer is Disinvestments **

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**** When the government sells only a part of its equity share capital of a public sector undertaking (PSU) but retains the majority stake, it's known as Disinvestment or Partial Disinvestment. The government maintains overall control of the company because it continues to hold a majority (50% plus one share) of the company's voting rights.**

Disinvestment, also referred to as divestment, has been used by governments worldwide as a part of their economic reform processes for various reasons:

 
• **Reducing Fiscal Burden: **Disinvestment helps reduce the financial burden on the government resulting from inefficient PSUs. As such, it assists in resource allocation from low-productivity sectors to high-productivity areas.
 
• **Improving Public Finances: **The process generates significant sums of money, which can then be used to close budget deficits, reduce debt, or finance other socio-economic programs.
 
• **Enhancing Company Performance: **When shares are sold to the general public or institutional investors, it typically leads to improved managerial performance and operational efficiency due to increased scrutiny and greater performance expectations.
 
• **Attracting Investment: **Disinvestment can be an initial step towards inviting more private and foreign investments. It signals a liberal economic environment, which can result in capital inflows from outside sources.
 
• **Promoting Public Ownership: **Disinvestment involves the sale of shares to the general public and institutional investors, thereby promoting a culture of investing.
 
• **Market Discipline: **It fosters a climate of market discipline and allows markets to have a significant role in resource allocation.

However, it's important to note that disinvestment, while providing several advantages, also attracts controversy and opposition. Critics often argue that disinvestment could lead to job losses, exacerbate income inequality, and expose critically important sectors to market volatility. Given this, how the process of disinvestment is managed becomes crucially important.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__** __Here are a few more points on disinvestment:__

 
• **Strategic Disinvestment: **This type of disinvestment involves selling a substantial portion of the Government's shareholding in a PSU while ceding management control. This is usually carried out in cases where the government wants to withdraw from non-core businesses.
 
• **Strengthening the Stock Market:** Disinvestment processes can significantly contribute to the deepening of the stock markets if PSU shares are sold on the stock exchange. It also fosters a more robust corporate governance framework and enhances the transparency and accountability of the PSUs.
 
• **Resolving Underutilization Issues: **PSUs often have considerable underutilized capacity. Disinvestment, particularly when followed by privatization, often leads to the better utilization of such capacities.
 
• **Rapid Industrial Growth: **The exposure to market competition forces PSUs to become more professional, efficient, and competitive. This accelerates the overall industrial growth of the country.
 
• **Check on Government Interference: **Disinvestment can also lead to the reduction of unnecessary interference by the government in the functioning of PSUs. Hence, the firms will be able to function in a more autonomous and competitive environment.
 
• **Improving Public Service Delivery: **The funds raised through disinvestment can be redirected toward improving public services. These might include areas such as public health, education, and infrastructure development.
 
• **Modernization of Firms:** If PSUs get disinvested, new private owners bring in the latest technology for the modernization of those units. Consequently, the productivity and efficiency of these firms increase significantly.

While disinvestment brings several potential benefits, careful thought and planning need to be undertaken so that the interests of all stakeholders, including employees, are considered, and the strategic interests of the nation are not compromised.

questions.question:
What is constant along an isoquant?

i. Level of Labour

ii. Level of Capital
questions.solution:
**The correct answer is Neither (i) nor (ii)**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• ** Neither the level of labor (i) nor capital (ii) is constant along an isoquant.**
 
• An isoquant represents all combinations of two inputs, often labor (L) and capital (K), that yield the same level of output. Therefore, the only thing that remains constant along an isoquant is the quantity of output produced.
 
• As you move along an isoquant, the amounts of labor and capital used in production change, but the total output remains the same. For instance, a firm may decide to use more labor and less capital, or vice versa, but if it is still on the same isoquant, the total level of output will be constant.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**__ Here are some additional points about isoquants:__

 
• Shape: Isoquants, similar to indifference curves in consumer theory, are downward-sloping and convex to the origin. This represents the tradeoff between the two inputs—capital and labor—and reflects the principle of diminishing marginal returns.
 
• Marginal Rate of Technical Substitution (MRTS): The slope of the isoquant at any point is known as the MRTS. This refers to the ratio at which a firm can substitute between two inputs while maintaining the same level of output.
 
• Contour Lines of a Production Function: Just as topographical maps have contour lines indicating different elevations, isoquants can be thought of as contour lines of a production function. Each isoquant represents a particular level of output.
 
• Isoquant Map: A map of isoquants for different levels of output is known as an isoquant map.
 
• Non-intersection: No two isoquants can intersect each other. Each isoquant corresponds to a different level of output, meaning a point cannot simultaneously yield two different levels of output.
 
• Distance from the Origin: Isoquants that are further from the origin represent higher levels of output, just as indifference curves further from the origin represent higher levels of utility.

The concept of isoquants is fundamental for understanding how firms make decisions about the optimal combination of inputs, given their prices, to produce a certain level of output. This decision, made at the point where the isoquant is tangent to the firm's budget constraint, plays a crucial role in cost minimization and profit maximization.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__** An isoquant is a contour line drawn through the set of points at which the same quantity of output is produced while changing the quantities of two or more inputs. It is a graphical representation of a production function, often used to depict the combination of inputs (usually capital and labor) that will produce a certain level of output.

The term "isoquant" comes from the prefix 'iso' meaning 'equal' and 'quant' referring to quantity. Therefore, an isoquant represents all combinations of inputs that yield the same ("iso") quantity ("quant").

**Key characteristics of isoquants include:**

 
• They are downward sloping (from left to right), representing that if the use of one input decreases, the use of another input must increase to maintain the same level of output.
 
• They are convex to the origin. This characteristic reflects the law of diminishing marginal rates of technical substitution, which states that as more of one input is used, keeping output constant, increasingly larger amounts of the other input must be given up.
 
• Isoquants cannot intersect. Each isoquant represents a different level of output, and a point in space cannot correspond to two different levels of output.
 
• The farther an isoquant is from the origin, the greater the level of output it represents.

questions.question: ____________ monetary policy is adopted when it is believed that higher interest rates are needed, usually to combat inflation or restrain rapid economic growth.
questions.solution:
**The correct answer is Hawkish**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• ** When higher interest rates are implemented to combat inflation or restrain economic growth, the monetary policy stance is referred to as "Hawkish."**
 
• **The hawkish approach stresses the importance of controlling inflation over stimulating economic growth. Typically, a hawkish monetary policy would involve increasing interest rates or otherwise removing money from circulation to curb inflation. This can slow economic growth because it tends to decrease borrowing and spending by both consumers and businesses due to higher interest rates**.
 
• Central banks raise the benchmark interest rate when they wish to follow a hawkish policy. This is done to reduce the amount of money and credit in the economy, thus fighting inflationary pressures.
 
• On the other hand, a "Dovish" stance prioritizes boosting the economy and reducing unemployment over the containment of inflation. Under dovish policies, interest rates are typically lowered to stimulate economic growth.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** __Here are some additional points related to hawkish monetary policy:__

 
• **Currency Value: **A hawkish monetary policy can cause the value of the country's currency to rise due to the higher interest rates, which can attract foreign investors seeking higher returns.
 
• **Effect on Stock Market: **Higher interest rates typically make borrowing more expensive, which can reduce corporate profits, potentially leading to a decline in the stock market. However, the effect on the market is also dependent on a range of other factors and economic indicators.
 
• **Long-Term Stability:** While a hawkish policy can slow down economic growth in the short term, it can contribute to long-term economic stability by preventing the economy from overheating and keeping inflation at a moderate level.
 
• **Effect on Debt: **Higher interest rates make it more costly for governments, corporations, and individuals to borrow and service their debt. This could lead to a reduction in overall debt levels, but it could also put a strain on those who have high debt burdens.
 
• **Policy Statements: **It's worth noting that often, the central bank doesn't even need to take action in order for their stance to affect the economy. Simply signaling a hawkish stance in policy statements can influence economic behavior, as markets adjust their expectations on the future path of interest rates.
 
• **Unintended Consequences: **While a hawkish policy is intended to curb inflation, there could be unintended side effects, such as exacerbating a downturn during an economic slowdown or causing deflation if overdone.

questions.question: As per the 15th Finance Commission final report, submitted on 9 November 2020, the Commission has recommended that ______________ of the net proceeds of Union taxes should be shared with the States.

• **Role of Finance Commission:** The Finance Commission is a constitutional body that is set up every five years to recommend measures and methods on how revenues, which come under the purview of the Union Government (like taxes), need to be distributed between the Centre and States.
 
• **Composition: **The Finance Commission is composed of a Chairman and four other members who are appointed by the President of India.
 
• **Criteria for Allocation:** The funds are allocated based on several criteria, which can include each state's population, area, forest and ecology, tax effort, fiscal capacity, income distance, and demographic performance.

questions.question:
A perfectly elastic supply curve means:

i. A horizontal supply curve

ii. Price Elasticity of Supply = Infinity
questions.solution:
**The correct answer is Both (i) and (ii)**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**** Both statements (i) and (ii) are accurate descriptions of a perfectly elastic supply curve.**

__
 
• ** A Horizontal Supply Curve: **A perfectly elastic supply curve is represented by a horizontal line where the price is constant regardless of the quantity supplied. It indicates that producers are willing to supply any amount of the good at one price, but nothing at any other price.
 
• ** Price Elasticity of Supply = Infinity: **When supply is perfectly elastic, the price elasticity of supply, which measures the responsiveness of the quantity supplied to a change in price, is indeed infinity. This is because even a very small change in price leads to an infinitely large change in the quantity supplied. In reality, perfectly elastic supply is more of a theoretical construct and is rarely observed because it requires that suppliers have the flexibility to ramp up production immediately and without limit in response to even a tiny increase in price and cease production completely in response to even a small decrease in price.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** **Here are some additional points about perfectly elastic supply:**

 
• **Industry Implication: **Perfectly elastic supply situations are more likely to apply to industries where it's easy to rapidly increase or decrease production without significant costs.
 
• **Extreme Case: **Perfectly elastic supply is an extreme case, often more theoretical than practical. Most real-world markets will exhibit some degree of elasticity, but not to the extent of being perfectly elastic.
 
• **Zero Revenue:** If a firm attempts to charge more than the going price in a market with a perfectly elastic supply, it will find no buyers, and its revenue will drop to zero.
 
• **Infinite Quantity: **Conversely, if it lowers the price, there is theoretically no limit to the quantity it could sell.
 
• **Product Homogeneity:** Perfect elasticity is more likely in markets where the product is identical across suppliers, like in perfectly competitive markets. Here, buyers don't differentiate between products based on the brand or other characteristics. If a seller charges even slightly more, buyers will switch to a competitor's product.
 
• **No Seller Control Over Price: **Producers are price takers in a market with a perfectly elastic supply, as they have no control over the price and must accept the market price.
 
• **Perfect Information:** Such situations also assume perfect information, where everyone in the market is fully informed about prices, quality, and production costs.
 
• **Limitless Stock:** A perfectly elastic supply assumes that producers have limitless stock and can supply any amount at a given price. As is evident, there are very few, if any, real-world examples of this — making it largely a theoretical concept.

questions.solution:
**The correct answer is (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv)**

**(i) It audits all receipts into and expenditures from the Consolidated Fund of India and each State and Union Territory having a Legislative Assembly.**

**(ii) The CAG audits all transactions, both related to the Contingency Funds and Public Accounts of the Union and the States.**

**(iii) It also audits the receipts and expenditures of bodies or authorities substantially financed from Union or State revenues.**

**(iv) Upon request, the CAG audits accounts of specific bodies or authorities.**

Therefore, all the provided options (i), (ii), (iii), and (iv) are indeed functions of the CAG in accordance with the designated act.

• The CAG is a constitutional body, provided under Article 148 of the Indian Constitution, tasked with auditing all receipts and expenditures of the Government of India and the state governments, including those of bodies and authorities substantially financed by the government.
 
• In the Indian parliamentary system, the CAG plays an essential role in maintaining the accountability of the government to the Parliament and State legislatures by reporting on the economy, efficiency, and effectiveness of government operations.
 
• The CAG can audit any body or authority when requested, but the request must come from the President or Governor, as per the powers conferred by the legislation. This provides an additional avenue for ensuring financial oversight over various entities in the country beyond regular government bonds.
 
• Besides financial audits, the CAG also conducts compliance audits (to determine the extent of compliance by the entity with applicable laws, rules, regulations, and procedures) and performance audits (which evaluate the efficiency, effectiveness, and economy of certain projects, programs, or schemes).
 
• The CAG's reports are taken very seriously and are tabled in the Parliament and, in the case of the State Government, in the State Legislative Assemblies. A Public Accounts Committee examines these reports, providing an additional layer of scrutiny over government spending.
 
• While the role of the CAG is primarily that of a watchdog to ensure accountability and transparency, the body does not have any punitive powers. After presenting its findings, it is up to the Parliament or the media/public to hold the government accountable.

These additional points highlight the importance of the CAG in maintaining financial discipline and accountability in public administration in India

questions.question: When an economy is operating inside the production possibility curve, it indicates that:
questions.solution:
**The correct answer is potential output > actual output **

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the context of a production possibility curve (also known as production possibility frontier, PPF), if an economy is operating inside the curve, it indicates underutilization of resources or inefficiency, meaning actual output is less than potential output.
 
• The PPF is a diagram that represents all possible combinations of two different goods or services that can be produced by an economy under the conditions of perfect resource allocation, given the current state of technology and productivity.
 
• So if an economy is operating at a point on the curve, it is said to be using its resources efficiently and to their full potential—actual output equals potential output. If operating inside the curve, there's productive inefficiency, as the economy could produce more goods and services by better leveraging available resources.
 
• Meanwhile, a point outside the curve represents an unachievable combination of goods with the economy's existing resources and technology—it's beyond the economy's current production capability. However, economies can move outside the curve as a result of implementing improvements, like technological advancements or better education and training, that increase productive capacity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** Absolutely, Here are some additional points regarding the condition when an economy is operating inside the production possibility curve (PPF):

 
• **Unemployment: **An economy operating inside the PPF often implies a high level of unemployment. Since not all resources are fully utilized, it indicates that some labor remains idle.
 
• **Economic Recession: **Operating inside the PPF could be indicative of an economic recession, where reduced demand for goods and services leads to less production and higher unemployment.
 
• **Scope for Improvement: **The fact that an economy is operating inside the PPF also indicates that there's scope for growth and improved efficiency. By adopting better technologies, training its workforce, or investing in capital goods, the economy can move towards the curve, indicating an efficient utilization of resources.
 
• **Wastage of Resources: **If an economy is operating inside the PPF, it might indicate wastage or poor management of resources. This could be due to poor governance or corruption.
 
• **Sub-optimal Production Mix:** Not only can inefficiency lead to operation inside the PPF, but it could also result from producing a sub-optimal mix of goods. Even if an economy is utilizing all its resources, if they're not allocated efficiently between different sectors of production, it will lead to operation within the PPF.
 
• **Economic Development: **For economies operating inside the PPF, the goal will be to enact policies and encourage behaviors which will push the output towards the boundary of the PPF, bettering the economic development of that region or country.

questions.question: The law of demand holds true when:

options.text: prices of related goods are allowed to change
tastes and preferences of consumers are not constant
own price of the commodity is assumed to be constant
all determinants of demand, other than own price of the commodity, remain constant

questions.solution:
**The correct answer is all determinants of demand, other than own price of the commodity, remain constant**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The law of demand states that all else being equal, as the price of a commodity or service increases, the quantity demanded will decrease, and vice versa. This is also known as the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded.
 
• This law is based on the assumption of "ceteris paribus", which means "all else being equal" in Latin. This assumption allows us to focus on the relationship between price and quantity demanded while ignoring other factors that could complicate the analysis.
 
• The other factors that could affect demand include income levels, prices of substitute goods, prices of complementary goods, expectations about future prices, demographic factors, and consumer tastes and preferences.
 
• For example, if we were trying to understand how the demand for apples changes when the price of apples changes, we'd have to assume that the consumers' incomes, the price of other fruits, consumer preferences for apples, etc., all remain constant or else those changes could impact the demand as well.
 
• Thus, the law of demand holds true when all determinants of demand, other than its own price, remain constant.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__** __Here are some additional insights related to the law of demand:__

 
• The law of demand is represented graphically with the demand curve, which slopes downwards from left to right. This graphical representation visually shows the inverse relationship between the price of a good or service and the quantity demanded.
 
• The law of demand is essentially a reflection of the consumer behavior of rational self-interest. When the price of goods rises, consumers tend to buy less because they are trying to get the most utility (satisfaction or need fulfillment) out of their limited budget, and vice versa.
 
• In certain cases, demand doesn't obey the law of demand. These are called Giffen goods and Veblen goods. In the case of Giffen goods (named after economist Robert Giffen), when price rises, people consume more - these tend to be inferior goods, for example, staple foods like bread or rice in very poor countries. Veblen goods (named after economist Thorstein Veblen) are luxury goods, where higher prices actually make the goods more desirable, encouraging more consumption.
 
• The law of demand also plays a crucial role in market equilibrium. It helps set the market price by interacting with the law of supply, and the point where the demand and supply curves meet is considered the market equilibrium.
 
• The concept of elasticity is closely linked to the law of demand. Price elasticity of demand measures the responsiveness of the quantity demanded to a change in the price. Some goods are highly elastic, meaning that a small price change can have a big impact on demand, while others are inelastic, meaning that demand doesn't change much when the price does.
 
• The law of demand is a fundamental principle of economics that helps businesses, governments, and individuals understand market dynamics, set prices, and predict responses to changes in price. However, it's important to remember that this law is a simplification of complex real-world phenomena and may not always apply due to other external factors and changing preferences.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT?

options.text: When the real exchange rate is one, the countries are said to be in purchasing power parity.
Nominal Exchange Rate is the price of one unit of foreign currency in terms of domestic currency.
When exports exceed imports, there is a trade deficit.
The Balance of Payments records a country's transactions with the rest of the world.

questions.solution:
**The correct answer is When exports exceed imports, there is a trade deficit.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When a country's exports exceed its imports, it has a trade surplus, not a deficit. A trade surplus means the value of goods and services a country sells to other nations (exports) is greater than what it buys (imports) from them.
 
• On the other hand, a trade deficit occurs when a country's imports exceed its exports. This means the country is buying more goods and services from other nations than it sells to them.
 
• In simplistic terms, a trade surplus can be viewed as a sign of a nation's economic success because it is selling more than it's buying, whereas a trade deficit might suggest the opposite. However, the reality is much more complex, and having a trade surplus or deficit can have both pros and cons, depending on the country's specific economic situation and policy goals.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**__ Some additional points on trade surpluses and deficits:__

 
• **Balance of Payments: **The terms trade surplus and deficit are part of a country's balance of payments, which includes not only trade in goods and services but also capital transfers and financial transactions. While a trade surplus adds to the balance of payments, a deficit subtracts from it.
 
• **Economic Performance: **A trade surplus is often seen as a sign of economic strength, and a deficit as a sign of weakness. However, this is an oversimplification. For example, a trade deficit can occur during periods of strong economic growth, when a country's businesses and consumers are buying more goods from overseas. Conversely, a trade surplus could occur during an economic downturn, when there is lower domestic demand for foreign goods.
 
• **Currency Implications: **Trade balances can affect the value of a country's currency in the foreign exchange markets. A sustained trade surplus can put upward pressure on a country's currency value, while a sustained trade deficit can put downward pressure on it.
 
• **Impact on Domestic Industries: **Constant trade deficits may harm domestic industries as they have to compete with cheaper or better foreign goods. On the other hand, continuous trade surpluses might lead to protectionist policies which can hinder competition and innovation in the long run.
 
• **Debt Levels:** Countries with large and persistent trade deficits often need to borrow from other countries to finance their deficits. This can increase the country's overall debt levels and make it more vulnerable to economic crises.
 
• **Politics and Trade Policy: **Trade surpluses and deficits can have significant impacts on politics and the development of trade policies. For instance, countries facing trade deficits may be more inclined to implement protectionist policies, such as tariffs and quotas, to protect domestic industries. On the other hand, those with trade surpluses might face pressure from other nations to open their markets more.

questions.question: The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003, was assented to on ____________ and commenced with effect from ____________.
questions.solution:
**The correct answer is 26 August 2003; 5 July 2004**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act (FRBM), 2003 was indeed assented to by the President of India on August 26, 2003, but the act came into effect on July 5, 2004. This legislation aimed to ensure fiscal discipline in the country by setting targets for the Government of India to establish financial stability.
 
• The FRBM Act mandates the government to place three documents before the parliament along with the Union Budget - the Medium Term Fiscal Policy Statement, the Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement, and the Macroeconomic Framework Statement. These documents present the government's plans for fiscal responsibility over the next three years.
 
• The purpose of the FRBM Act, of 2003 was to ensure prudent fiscal management and fiscal stability by progressive elimination of the revenue deficit, reduce fiscal deficit, restrain borrowings, debt, and inflation, and ensure that macroeconomic stability through prudent fiscal management is maintained.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**__ Here are some additional points about the FRBM Act:__

 
• **Key Provisions: **The act set clear targets for the central government: reduce fiscal deficit to 3% of GDP and eliminate the revenue deficit by March 31, 2008. By doing so, it aimed to make the government more responsible for its revenue and expenditure management.
 
• **Key Documents: **The Act mandates the government to present three key documents to the Parliament annually: A Medium-term Fiscal Policy Statement, a Macroeconomic Framework Statement, and a Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement. These documents outline a three-year rolling target for specific fiscal indicators.
 
• **Review Committee: **The FRBM Act, 2003 mandated the setting up of a review committee to oversee the operation of its provisions, to suggest necessary changes, and to detail any shortfalls in achieving the stated objectives.
 
• **Escape Clauses: **The legislation contains "escape clauses" for deviations from the prescribed targets due to explicit unforeseen events like national calamity, national security, and structural reforms.
 
• **Amendments: **The targets set by the FRBM Act, 2003 have been revised over the years depending on the recommendations of different finance commissions and the prevailing economic condition. The government has set revised targets on the basis of the NK Singh Committee recommendations, which propose a glide path to bring down the fiscal deficit to 2.5% of GDP by 2023.
 
• **COVID-19 and FRBM Act: **Due to the economic fallout from the COVID-19 pandemic, the Government of India suspended the FRBM Act in 2020-21 and 2021-22 since the unprecedented situation necessitated high government spending for relief measures and stimulus packages. This divulges from the fiscal prudence path laid out by the Act, highlighting how in extraordinary times, the fiscal deficit targets under the FRBM Act can be relaxed.

The implementation of the Act, however, has been a challenge. The government has found it difficult to stick to the targets because of various challenges including oil price volatility, revenue shortfall, and higher expenditure requirements due to rising developmental needs.

Nonetheless, the FRBM Act is considered a significant step towards the institution of sound fiscal practices in India and ensuring long-term macroeconomic stability.
